name: Auriculotherapy

card.summary: Ear-point stimulation (needles, seeds, staples or electrical devices) that some people use hoping to reduce appetite and support weight loss or skin changes.
card.aka: ear acupuncture, auricular acupuncture, ear seeds
card.note: Ear stapling carries infection and cartilage risks; appearance claims are untested.

quick.overview:
Auriculotherapy is the practice of stimulating points on the outer ear, based on the idea that the ear maps the whole body. Within looksmaxxing it appears mainly as an appetite and weight-control tool, where people hope reduced hunger leads to a leaner face and body, and in skin-related claims.
Research on it has mostly examined pain, anxiety, sleep and labour. A 1995 rat study looked at ear stimulation and feeding-related brain activity; trials of auriculotherapy for facial appearance are not among those reviewed here.
quick.how: Methods include acupuncture needles, small seeds taped to ear points (auricular acupressure), semi-permanent studs or staples, lasers, and electrical ear-clip devices. Practitioners typically choose points on a standard ear chart.
quick.risks: Reported concerns focus on ear stapling, which a 2010 article called risky and unproven and which a US state medical board has opposed. Needles and implants in cartilage carry infection risk.

lead: Auriculotherapy, also called ear acupuncture or auricular therapy, is an alternative-medicine practice based on the idea that the outer ear is a micro-system reflecting the whole body, so that stimulating particular points can influence distant organs.[1] The French neurologist Paul Nogier developed it in 1957, and it reached China in 1958, where it was incorporated into traditional Chinese medicine.[1]

In appearance communities it is mentioned mainly for appetite suppression and weight loss, via ear seeds or ear stapling, with the chain being less hunger, lower body fat, and a leaner face and body.[1] Some wellness practitioners also offer ear-point treatments marketed for skin.
Research has examined auriculotherapy for pain, stress, anxiety and depression, insomnia and labour; reviewers describe the studies as often limited by methodological weaknesses.[2][3][4]

chain: Ear points are stimulated with seeds, needles or staples
Less food intake and a leaner face and body
angle.text: People use ear seeds or ear points hoping to curb appetite and so lose body fat, which shows up in the face. The appearance claims have not been tested in trials in the cited literature.

infobox: Needles, seeds, staples, laser, electrical stimulation

paras: Nogier's chart projects an inverted fetus onto the ear: the lobe corresponds to the head and face, the scapha to the upper limbs, the antihelix to the trunk and lower limbs, and the concha to internal organs.[1] Wikipedia notes the mappings lack scientific support.[1]

Modern variants include battlefield acupuncture, developed by Richard Niemtzow in 2001 for pain, which uses gold semi-permanent needles at up to five ear sites.[1] Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation devices are a related electrical approach, with a review noting a lack of standardisation across devices.[5]

Proponents say ear points related to hunger and the stomach can be stimulated with seeds, needles or staples to reduce appetite. Ear stapling, in which a staple is placed in ear cartilage, is promoted for weight loss, smoking cessation and stress.[1]

A 1995 study in normal and obese rats recorded feeding-related hypothalamic neuron activity during auricular stimulation, reporting that auriculotherapy is known to sometimes produce weight reduction in obese patients.[6]

A 1984 controlled crossover study by Ronald Melzack in JAMA found no pain reduction at auriculotherapy points versus control points, which the author attributed to placebo.[7][1] A 2010 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined auriculotherapy for pain,[8] and a 2018 overview of systematic reviews assessed its effectiveness across conditions.[9]

A 2020 systematic review of 24 studies found 22 reported a positive effect on stress, anxiety or depression, with the authors noting methodological weaknesses.[2] Meta-analyses have examined labour pain and duration.[3]
A 2010 article called ear stapling risky and unproven, and the Iowa Board of Medicine has taken a position against it.[1]

Human trials of auriculotherapy have covered pain, anxiety and depression, insomnia, labour and cancer-related symptoms.[2][3][4][8] No trials on facial appearance or skin were found. Weight-related work cited here is the rat study.[6]

timeline.event: Paul Nogier develops auricular acupuncture in France.[1]
Melzack's JAMA crossover study reports no pain relief beyond control.[7]
